topics.title: What is a Computer Network? LAN, WAN, MAN & Client-Server vs P2P
topics.what_is_it: A Computer Network is an interconnected system of computing devices that share data, resources, and communication channels using standardized communication protocols.
topics.simple_explanation:
Computer networks span different geographical scales:
- **LAN (Local Area Network)**: Connects devices in a close physical proximity (home, office building, or school). High bandwidth, low latency, owned by a single organization.
- **WAN (Wide Area Network)**: Spans cities, countries, or continents (e.g. The Internet). Managed by multiple ISPs.
- **MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)**: Spans a city or university campus.
- **Internet & ISP**: The Internet is a global 'network of networks'. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) provide Tier-1, Tier-2, and Tier-3 routing access.
- **Client-Server Architecture**: Dedicated server hosts services; clients request data (e.g., Web Browsers querying Nginx).
- **Peer-to-Peer (P2P)**: Nodes act as both clients and servers sharing resources directly (e.g. BitTorrent).
- **Network Topologies**: Physical layout — **Star** (connected to central switch), **Mesh** (full redundant interconnectivity for fault tolerance), **Bus**, and **Ring**.
topics.real_world_analogy: A LAN is like an internal office intercom. A WAN is the global telephone network. Client-Server is like ordering food at a restaurant (Waiter/Server brings food to Customer/Client). Peer-to-Peer is like a potluck dinner where everyone brings and shares food directly with each other.
why_it_exists: Enable high-speed communication and resource sharing across local and global distances.
Establish scalable client-server and distributed network architectures.
tech_world: AWS Virtual Private Clouds (VPC) logically isolate cloud resources into LAN subnets spanning global WAN regions.
key_points: LAN = Local (Home/Office); WAN = Global (Internet); MAN = Metropolitan City.
Client-Server: Centralized server responds to client requests.
Peer-to-Peer (P2P): Decentralized nodes serve and request data directly.
Star Topology: Most common LAN design using a central Switch.
Mesh Topology: Highest fault tolerance with multiple redundant links.
interview_focus: What is the structural difference between Client-Server and Peer-to-Peer architectures?
Why is Mesh topology preferred for high-availability core data center backbones?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between Client-Server and Peer-to-Peer (P2P) network architectures?
interview_questions.answer: In Client-Server architecture, central servers maintain resources and process client requests (asymmetric roles). In P2P architecture, every node (peer) acts as both a client and a server, downloading and uploading data chunks concurrently without a central bottleneck.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Network Topologies:
Star:    [Node] -- [Switch] -- [Node]
Mesh:    [Node] <===> [Node] <===> [Node] (All interconnected redundant links)
quickRevisionNotes: LAN = Local; WAN = Global Internet.
Star topology relies on a central switch; Mesh provides redundant paths.

topics.title: Network Data Units (Packet, Frame, Segment, Datagram) & Metrics
topics.what_is_it: Network Data Units define data encapsulation formats across protocol layers, while Performance Metrics evaluate throughput, delay, and loss.
topics.simple_explanation:
As data travels down the network stack, each layer wraps it in its own header (Encapsulation):
- **Segment**: Transport Layer TCP data unit (contains Source/Destination Ports).
- **Datagram**: Transport Layer UDP data unit or Network Layer connectionless packet.
- **Packet**: Network Layer IP data unit (contains Source/Destination IP Addresses).
- **Frame**: Data Link Layer Ethernet data unit (contains Source/Destination MAC Addresses).
- **Bits**: Physical Layer electrical pulses or light signals.

**Performance Metrics**:
- **Bandwidth**: Theoretical maximum capacity of a network link per second (e.g. 1 Gbps).
- **Throughput**: Actual rate of successful data delivery over a channel.
- **Latency**: One-way delay for a packet to travel from source to destination.
- **RTT (Round Trip Time)**: Total time for a packet to travel to destination AND return an ACK.
- **Jitter**: Fluctuation or variability in packet arrival latency (causes stutter in video calls).
- **Packet Loss**: Percentage of transmitted packets dropped by congested routers.
topics.real_world_analogy: Bandwidth is a 6-lane highway width. Throughput is the actual number of cars passing per minute. Latency is the travel time to a destination city. RTT is driving there and returning home. Jitter is erratic traffic stop-and-go delays. Packet loss is a box falling off a delivery truck.
why_it_exists: Standardize data encapsulation layers so protocols remain independent.
Quantify network Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for latency and packet delivery.
tech_world: Monitoring tools (Datadog, New Relic) measure RTT and Jitter to detect network bottlenecks affecting microservices.
key_points: Segment = TCP (Transport Layer); Datagram = UDP / IP.
Packet = IP (Network Layer); Frame = Ethernet (Data Link Layer).
RTT = Time to destination + return ACK time.
Jitter = Latency variance (critical for VoIP & Gaming).
Throughput is always <= Bandwidth.
interview_focus: Explain the difference between Bandwidth, Throughput, and Latency.
What is RTT and why does high RTT slow down TCP throughput?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between Latency, RTT, and Jitter?
interview_questions.answer: Latency is one-way transit time. RTT (Round Trip Time) is the total time for a packet to reach the destination and return an ACK. Jitter is the variance or fluctuation in latency between consecutive packets.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Encapsulation Flow:
[ Application Data ]
  --> [ TCP Header | Data ]           (Segment - Layer 4)
  --> [ IP Header | TCP | Data ]       (Packet - Layer 3)
  --> [ MAC Header | IP | TCP | Data ] (Frame - Layer 2)
  --> 10110100101...                   (Bits - Layer 1)
quickRevisionNotes: Data -> Segment (L4) -> Packet (L3) -> Frame (L2) -> Bits (L1).
RTT includes return ACK transit time.

topics.title: The OSI 7-Layer Model vs TCP/IP Model
topics.what_is_it: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) 7-Layer Model and TCP/IP 4-Layer Model provide conceptual frameworks for network protocol communication.
topics.simple_explanation:
Network communication is divided into modular abstraction layers:

**OSI 7-Layer Model**:
1. **Application (Layer 7)**: User interaction protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH, FTP).
2. **Presentation (Layer 6)**: Data formatting, compression, and encryption (TLS/SSL, JPEG, JSON).
3. **Session (Layer 5)**: Session establishment and management (RPC, NetBIOS).
4. **Transport (Layer 4)**: End-to-end process communication, ports, error recovery (TCP, UDP).
5. **Network (Layer 3)**: Logical host addressing and internet routing (IP, ICMP, Routers).
6. **Data Link (Layer 2)**: Node-to-node frame delivery on physical medium (Ethernet, MAC, Switches, ARP).
7. **Physical (Layer 1)**: Transmission of raw binary bits over cables/radio (Cables, Wi-Fi, Voltage).

**TCP/IP 4-Layer Model (Practical Standard)**:
- **Application Layer** (Combines OSI 7, 6, 5)
- **Transport Layer** (OSI 4)
- **Internet Layer** (OSI 3)
- **Network Access / Link Layer** (Combines OSI 2, 1).
topics.real_world_analogy: Sending a letter: Application = Writing letter text. Presentation = Translating to English. Session = Writing formal letter structure. Transport = Choosing Express Tracked Mail. Network = Writing Recipient Address (IP). Data Link = Loading letter into delivery van (MAC). Physical = Driving the van on asphalt roads.
why_it_exists: Modularize network software so changing Layer 2 (Wi-Fi to Ethernet) doesn't break Layer 7 (Browser/HTTP).
Establish global protocol standards for multi-vendor hardware interoperability.
tech_world: Network firewalls are categorized by layer: Layer 3/4 Firewalls (filter IP/Ports) vs Layer 7 Web Application Firewalls (WAF filter HTTP payloads).
key_points: OSI Layers: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.
TCP/IP Layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access.
Ports = Layer 4 (Transport); IP Addresses = Layer 3 (Network); MAC = Layer 2 (Data Link).
interview_focus: Compare the OSI 7-layer model with the TCP/IP 4-layer model.
At which OSI layers do Switches, Routers, and Web Application Firewalls operate?

interview_questions.question: At which OSI layers do Hubs, Switches, Routers, and Web Application Firewalls (WAF) operate?
interview_questions.answer: Hubs operate at Layer 1 (Physical). Switches operate at Layer 2 (Data Link - MAC Addresses). Routers operate at Layer 3 (Network - IP Addresses). WAFs operate at Layer 7 (Application - HTTP payloads).

topics.syntaxOrCode:
OSI vs TCP/IP Mapping:
OSI 7-Layer                     TCP/IP 4-Layer
[ 7. Application  ] \
[ 6. Presentation ]  ===> [ Application Layer ] (HTTP, DNS, TLS)
[ 5. Session      ] /
[ 4. Transport    ]  ===> [ Transport Layer   ] (TCP, UDP)
[ 3. Network      ]  ===> [ Internet Layer    ] (IP, ICMP)
[ 2. Data Link    ] \
[ 1. Physical     ]  ===> [ Network Access    ] (Ethernet, MAC)
quickRevisionNotes: OSI has 7 layers; TCP/IP has 4 practical layers.
Routers operate at Layer 3; Switches operate at Layer 2.

topics.title: Master Walkthrough: 'When I open google.com, what happens at each layer?'
topics.what_is_it: The definitive SDE interview walkthrough detailing every step from typing `google.com` in a browser to rendering the HTML page across the OSI/TCP-IP stack.
topics.simple_explanation:
This classic master interview question connects every major networking concept:

1. **User Types `google.com` & Presses Enter**:
   - Browser parses URL and checks **Browser Cache** -> **OS Cache** -> **`/etc/hosts`** for IP address.
2. **DNS Resolution Pipeline (Layer 7 Application)**:
   - If cache miss, OS sends DNS request to **Recursive Resolver** (ISP / 1.1.1.1).
   - Resolver queries **Root Server (`.`)** -> **TLD Server (`.com`)** -> **Authoritative Server (`google.com`)** to get IP `142.250.190.46`.
3. **ARP Resolution (Layer 2 Data Link)**:
   - OS checks local ARP cache for Default Gateway Router MAC. If missing, sends **ARP Request Broadcast** (`FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF`) to get Router MAC.
4. **TCP 3-Way Handshake (Layer 4 Transport)**:
   - Browser initiates TCP connection to `142.250.190.46:443`. Sends `SYN` -> Receives `SYN+ACK` -> Sends `ACK` (`ESTABLISHED` state).
5. **TLS 1.3 Handshake (Layer 6 Presentation)**:
   - Browser sends `ClientHello` key share. Server verifies SSL Certificate, returns `ServerHello`, and establishes symmetric AES encryption keys.
6. **HTTP GET Request & Server Response (Layer 7 Application)**:
   - Browser sends encrypted `GET / HTTP/1.1` request. Google Nginx/Envoy web server processes request and returns `200 OK` with HTML/JS payload.
7. **Browser Rendering**:
   - Browser receives HTML bytes, parses DOM tree, CSSOM tree, executes JavaScript, and renders page!
topics.real_world_analogy: Opening `google.com` is like ordering a book online: 1. Look up book ID in catalog (DNS). 2. Find local post office address (ARP). 3. Establish formal shipping contract with courier (TCP Handshake). 4. Lock package in tamper-proof container (TLS Encryption). 5. Ship package and receive book (HTTP Request/Response). 6. Unbox and read book (Browser Rendering).
why_it_exists: Demonstrates complete end-to-end understanding of web protocols, hardware, and client-server architectures.
tech_world: Senior SDE and System Design interviewers evaluate candidates based on the depth of detail in this walkthrough.
key_points: Step 1: URL Parsing & DNS Resolution (Layer 7).
Step 2: ARP Lookup for Gateway MAC (Layer 2).
Step 3: TCP 3-Way Handshake SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK (Layer 4).
Step 4: TLS 1.3 Handshake Key Exchange (Layer 6).
Step 5: HTTP GET Request & 200 OK Response (Layer 7).
Step 6: DOM/CSSOM Parsing & Screen Rendering.
interview_focus: Walk through every step of typing google.com and pressing Enter in a browser.
What happens if DNS fails? What happens if TCP Handshake times out?

interview_questions.question: What happens if the ARP cache doesn't contain the MAC address of the default gateway router when opening google.com?
interview_questions.answer: The operating system pauses IP packet transmission and broadcasts an ARP Request (`FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF`) asking 'Who has Default Gateway IP?'. The gateway router responds with an ARP Reply unicast containing its physical MAC address. The OS caches the MAC address and resumes sending the TCP SYN frame.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Execution Pipeline Flow:
[ Type google.com ] 
  --> [ DNS Lookup (Get IP) ] 
  --> [ ARP Lookup (Get Router MAC) ] 
  --> [ TCP 3-Way Handshake (Port 443) ] 
  --> [ TLS 1.3 Handshake (Encrypt) ] 
  --> [ HTTP GET Request ] 
  --> [ HTTP 200 OK Response ] 
  --> [ DOM Rendering ]
quickRevisionNotes: Flow: DNS -> ARP -> TCP Handshake -> TLS Handshake -> HTTP GET -> 200 OK -> Render.
DNS converts domain to IP; ARP converts IP to Gateway MAC.
